summary: Defines a community-based administrative framework for SNMP version 2, using simple community names for access control as SNMPv1 did. It was an experimental protocol and is now historic.

eli5.summary: A club where anyone who knows the secret password can ask the network devices questions. That is how this older management scheme decided who was allowed in.

how is snmpv2c different from snmpv1
what version number does community-based snmpv2 use
subtitle: How SNMP version 2 kept the old SNMPv1 community-name scheme for deciding who may talk to a device.

tldr.problem: SNMP version 2 was split across several documents and needed an administrative framework that says how messages are tied to access rules.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1901 reuses the SNMPv1 community-based framework, where each message carries a community name, and changes only the version number in the message wrapper plus a few small procedure updates.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Experimental, discusses no security issues, and is now classified as Historic.

today: RFC 1901 is classified as Historic. It was published as an Experimental protocol in January 1996 and its text says nothing about security beyond the community name carried in each message.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1901 defines the Community-based Administrative Framework for the SNMP version 2 framework (SNMPv2). The SNMPv2 framework itself is described in a set of companion documents, and it is derived from the original Internet-standard Network Management Framework, SNMPv1.

SNMPv1 consisted of three documents: RFC 1155 (the Structure of Management Information), RFC 1212 (a more concise way to describe managed objects) and RFC 1157 (the Simple Network Management Protocol). For coexistence between SNMPv1 and SNMPv2, the memo points to RFC 1908.
sections.eli5: There was an older version of the network-management language and a newer one. This memo explains how the newer one gets its rules for who is allowed to ask questions.

sections.title: Components of the SNMPv2 Framework
sections.content:
A management system has several nodes, each with a processing entity called an agent that can reach management instrumentation. It also has at least one management station and a management protocol that carries management information between agents and stations. Protocol operations run under an administrative framework that defines authentication, authorization, access control and privacy policies.

RFC 1901 lists the pieces of the framework and the document that defines each one:

  • Structure of Management Information (RFC 1902): a subset of ASN.1 with macros for module, object and notification definitions.
  • Textual conventions (RFC 1903): new types with a similar syntax but more precise meaning, for the convenience of people reading a MIB module.
  • Conformance statements (RFC 1904): compliance and capability notations, plus groups of related objects.
  • Protocol operations (RFC 1905): messages are a wrapper around a Protocol Data Unit (PDU).
  • Transport mappings (RFC 1906): how SNMPv2 maps onto transport domains. The mapping onto UDP is the preferred one, and systems that use other mappings should also provide proxy service to the UDP mapping.
  • Protocol instrumentation (RFC 1907): managed objects that describe the behavior of an SNMPv2 entity.
sections.eli5: The whole system is like a board game with a rulebook split into chapters. One chapter says how to name things, one says how to send messages, and so on. This memo is the chapter about who is allowed to play.

sections.title: The Community-based Administrative Framework
sections.content:
The administrative framework for SNMPv2 in this document is the same one defined for SNMPv1 in RFC 1157. It associates each message with a community. Using this framework with SNMP version 2 is commonly known as Community-based SNMPv2 (SNMPv2C).

The memo points to Section 3.2.5 of RFC 1157 for the concept of a community and Section 4.1 for the Elements of Procedure, and then applies three updates:

  • The types of access defined in RFC 1157 are updated by the SNMPv2 Structure of Management Information.
  • The Elements of Procedure gain the requirement to increment the relevant statistics counter defined in the SNMPv2 MIB.
  • The rule that a response must be sent from the same transport address the request was sent to is deleted, so a response can come from any transport address belonging to the agent.
sections.eli5: The new version keeps the old club rule: say the secret word and you are in. It only changes a few small details, like letting the answer come back from any of the agent's own mailboxes.

sections.title: The Message Wrapper
sections.content:
The form of a message is also taken from RFC 1157, with one exception: a new version number is used in the message wrapper. A new number is needed because SNMPv2 has new PDU types and error codes. The wrapper is a sequence of three parts:

  • version, which is 1 here (modified from RFC 1157);
  • community, the community name, as an octet string;
  • data, the PDUs defined in RFC 1905.

The authorizationError(16) value defined for the error-status component of an SNMPv2 PDU is unused with this framework. It may be used with future administrative frameworks.
sections.eli5: Every message is an envelope with three things inside: a version label, the secret word, and the actual question or answer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo's Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The only access control it describes is the community name carried in each message.
sections.eli5: The memo does not say anything about how safe the secret-word idea is.
